evidence_quotes.quote: This study evaluated the sustainability of a rural water point rehabilitation project that was carried out in Mwenezi (Masvingo Province), and Gwanda, Bulilima and Mangwe (Matabeleland South Province) districts by a local NGO.

The rehabilitation project involved repair and rehabilitation of existing boreholes as well as drilling of new boreholes. Workshops aimed at improving the technical, managerial, health and hygiene knowledge of villagers formed part of the programme.
Water point committees were reported to be in place by 76% (Mwenezi), 83% (Gwanda), 71% (Bulilima) and 71% (Mangwe) of respondents in the study area.

evidence_quotes.quote: Enforcement of contributions was reported to be carried out by traditional leaders.
The methods in this study included physical inspection of the water points by the study team and questionnaires.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 3, Section 4.1.1 Functioning and state of water points
evidence_quotes.quote: It was observed that some 14% of water points were not working in Mwenezi, 17% in Gwanda, 13% in Bulilima, and 25% in Mangwe.
Nevertheless, walking distance to a water point was reduced following the borehole rehabilitation project according to 83–100% of the responses in all districts.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household/community drinking-water service access via rehabilitated communal boreholes across four rural districts in Zimbabwe, including borehole functionality, seasonal water availability, and walking distance to water points.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because Sections 4.2 and 4.3 explicitly survey 'institutional arrangements' (existence and regular meetings of community Water Point Committees) and community O&M financing/traditional-leader contribution enforcement as project sustainability indicators. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no): the evaluated intervention/exposure is generic NGO project delivery and behavioural/training promotion (emergency borehole rehabilitation/drilling, O&M repair workshops, participatory health and hygiene education, and generic community participation). Although Section 4.3 briefly notes descriptively that 84%–93% of responses reported ad hoc breakdown contributions enforced by traditional leaders (with non-contributors generally continuing to abstract water), tariff/cost-recovery or enforcement rules are not analyzed as a mechanism governing water access, exclusion, or system reliability; access outcomes (reduced walking distance and pump functionality) are evaluated purely as outcomes of the NGO rehabilitation project.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data collected April–June 2005 via physical inspections of 144 rehabilitated boreholes and structured questionnaires administered to adult villagers across four districts.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports water access, availability, and reliability outcomes, including the proportion of non-functional/broken-down boreholes (13%–25%), breakdown frequency and repair timeliness, seasonal drying up (water availability), pump ease of operation, and perceived reduction in walking distance to a water point (83%–100%).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the geographic setting and water-point sample (144 rehabilitated boreholes across Mwenezi, Gwanda, Bulilima, and Mangwe districts, plus adult villagers aged 20+ using them, though exact interviewee N is not reported), the project exposure (NGO borehole rehabilitation and training programme), access/reliability outcomes, and a cross-sectional post-project field evaluation design.

study_design: Cross-sectional post-project field evaluation combining physical inspections of water points and structured villager questionnaires
population_and_sample: 144 rehabilitated rural water points (boreholes: 37 in Mwenezi, 41 in Gwanda, 38 in Bulilima, and 28 in Mangwe districts) and adult villagers (aged 20 years and older; exact respondent count not reported) abstracting water from those water points
exposure: NGO-implemented rural borehole rehabilitation and drilling project accompanied by operation and maintenance (O&M) and participatory health and hygiene education (PHHE) training workshops
outcome: Water point functionality and breakdown rates (13%–25% non-functional), seasonal water availability, ease of pump operation, perceived water quality, and perceived reduction in walking distance to a water point (83%–100% of respondents)
rationale: This empirical post-project evaluation inspects 144 rehabilitated boreholes and surveys rural water users across four districts in Zimbabwe regarding water point functionality, seasonal water availability, O&M and hygiene training workshops, Water Point Committees (WPCs), repair contributions, and walking distance (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because Sections 4.2 and 4.3 explicitly assess community institutional and financing arrangements (existence/meetings of WPCs and breakdown repair contributions). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): the study evaluates generic NGO project delivery, community participation, and O&M/hygiene training rather than analyzing how a legal, administrative, tariff/cost-recovery, or enforcement rule governs water access or reliability. Although Section 4.3 briefly notes that ad hoc breakdown contributions were enforced by traditional leaders while non-contributors continued to abstract water, cost-recovery or enforcement rules are not examined as an exposure affecting service access or breakdown outcomes.
